contentBody: **What should you keep when pasting a meeting transcript into an AI tool?**
option.1: Speaker names and their timestamps
option.2: Only the last five minutes of the meeting
option.3: Only the topic headings from the agenda
option.4: Nothing at all — delete all the names
answerExplanation: Names and timestamps let you trace any summary line back to the source.

contentBody: **A group first says "ship to everyone," then later agrees "ship to 10% first." What goes in the final decisions list?**
option.1: Both, listed as two separate decisions
option.2: Only "ship to everyone," the first statement
option.3: Neither one, because they conflict
option.4: Only the 10% rollout, with a note on the change
answerExplanation: The last word on a topic wins; note that the decision changed.

contentBody: **A task was raised but nobody agreed to own it. What should the action item say for the owner?**
option.1: Assign it to the person who raised it
option.2: "No owner agreed" with a clear flag
option.3: Assign it to the team manager instead
option.4: Leave it out of the list
answerExplanation: Flag the gap instead of guessing an owner.

contentBody: **Which prompt instruction best prevents invented details in a summary?**
option.1: "Make it sound confident, polished and professional"
option.2: "Be as creative as possible with the wording"
option.3: "Use only what is actually written in the text"
option.4: "Keep it as short as you possibly can"
answerExplanation: A source-only rule stops the AI filling gaps with plausible details.

contentBody: **A summary gives one task to the wrong person. Which of these checks should catch this?**
option.1: Checking the word count of the summary
option.2: Checking the tone used in the summary
option.3: Running a spell check on the whole summary
option.4: Comparing the owners with the source text
answerExplanation: Owners, dates, numbers and reversals are checked against the source text.

contentBody: **A transcript is too long for one single prompt. What can you do about it?**
option.1: Delete the middle section of the transcript so it fits
option.2: Paste only the start of it and ignore the rest
option.3: Summarise it section by section, then summarise the summaries
option.4: Wait until the transcript gets shorter by itself after some time
answerExplanation: Splitting long text into sections keeps the whole document in play.

contentBody: **What should belong in every single action item?**
option.1: The owner, action, and deadline
option.2: The mood, topic, and length
option.3: The date, venue, and weather
option.4: The title, font, and colour
answerExplanation: An action item names who does what by when.

contentBody: **A summary says "budget approved: ₹80,000." The transcript says ₹50,000. What kind of error is this?**
option.1: A small formatting issue in how it is laid out
option.2: A clear number mismatch with the source text
option.3: A problem with the tone of the writing
option.4: Just a personal style choice
answerExplanation: Every figure must match the source exactly.

contentBody: **Which of these tasks is the best candidate for an AI routine?**
option.1: A confidential salary query from staff
option.2: A one-off legal dispute with a client
option.3: A rare speech to the board
option.4: A weekly status update for the team
answerExplanation: Frequent, repeatable, low-to-medium risk tasks repay the setup.

contentBody: **What is a good reason to keep a task away from AI tools entirely?**
option.1: It is repetitive and follows a routine
option.2: It involves confidential or private data
option.3: It happens every single week without much variation
option.4: It follows a standard, set format
answerExplanation: Confidential or high-stakes work stays with you, or in an approved tool.

contentBody: **Which part of a prompt template changes each time you use it?**
option.1: The role you assign to the AI
option.2: The rules you set for the task
option.3: The input slot with new material
option.4: The output format you ask for each time
answerExplanation: The role, rules and format stay fixed; only the pasted material changes.

contentBody: **Why split a research task into several chained prompts?**
option.1: Each small step is much easier to check
option.2: AI tools always refuse long prompts
option.3: It always costs a lot less
option.4: It removes the need to review anything
answerExplanation: Small steps let you catch a wrong detail before it spreads.

contentBody: **A task takes 40 minutes by hand and 12 with AI. What keeps those 12 minutes trustworthy?**
option.1: Skipping the final review step to save time
option.2: A human check built into the whole routine
option.3: Writing a much longer and more detailed prompt
option.4: Switching to a different tool
answerExplanation: The saving comes from the draft, not from skipping the check.

contentBody: **Which type of task profile scores best for AI help?**
option.1: Rare, high-stakes, and highly confidential
option.2: Frequent, repeatable, and fairly low risk
option.3: Rare, unique, and highly confidential
option.4: One-off, high-stakes, and urgent
answerExplanation: Frequency and repeatability make a template worthwhile; low risk keeps checking light.

contentBody: **What exactly is an "input slot" in a prompt template?**
option.1: The box where the AI's reply appears
option.2: The name of the model you are using
option.3: The section holding the rules and the format
option.4: The marked blank where new material goes
answerExplanation: It is where you paste the material that changes each time.

contentBody: **You keep fixing the same mistake in your AI drafts. What should you do about it?**
option.1: Add a new rule to your saved template
option.2: Stop using AI for drafts altogether
option.3: Fix it by hand every single time
option.4: Switch to a new tool weekly
answerExplanation: Each repeated fix becomes a rule, so the template improves over time.

contentBody: **Which of these should you verify at the source before sending?**
option.1: A friendly greeting line at the start
option.2: A section heading somewhere in the draft
option.3: A direct quote from a named person
option.4: A bullet marker used in a list of points
answerExplanation: Quotes and citations are traced to the original, or removed.

contentBody: **You cannot verify a statistic the AI gave you. What do you do with it?**
option.1: Cut it, or clearly mark it unconfirmed
option.2: Keep it in, because it sounds right
option.3: Round it to be safe
option.4: Ask the AI to confirm its own claim
answerExplanation: If you cannot verify it, it does not go out as fact.

contentBody: **A draft says "Customers who complain just want freebies." What kind of risk is this?**
option.1: Outdated context in the draft
option.2: A simple formatting issue
option.3: A fabricated source citation
option.4: Biased, unsupported logic
answerExplanation: It is an unsupported generalisation, not a fact.

contentBody: **An AI quotes last year's price as the current price. What risk is this?**
option.1: Biased, unsupported logic
option.2: Outdated or stale context
option.3: A brand voice problem
option.4: A formatting problem
answerExplanation: The detail was true once but is no longer current.

contentBody: **A draft shouts in capitals but the house style is plain. Which review pass fixes it?**
option.1: The data fidelity pass
option.2: The compliance pass
option.3: The brand voice pass
option.4: The sourcing pass
answerExplanation: Tone, punctuation and style rules belong to the brand-voice pass.

contentBody: **What is the safest source for checking a figure in a draft?**
option.1: The original document it came from
option.2: The AI's own repeated answer
option.3: A colleague's memory of it
option.4: Any similar-looking website online
answerExplanation: A primary source is the original document, page or person.

contentBody: **An AI invents a source that sounds quite real. What is this called?**
option.1: A small formatting error only
option.2: A fact that is outdated
option.3: A hallucinated citation or reference
option.4: A mismatch with brand voice
answerExplanation: A fluent, specific reference that does not exist.

contentBody: **After rewriting a draft with AI, what must you do before sending it?**
option.1: Send it out right away
option.2: Trust it, since it was already checked once
option.3: Delete the old version of it
option.4: Check it again from scratch
answerExplanation: A rewrite can introduce new errors, so it needs its own check.
